Urban heat islands form when cities replace vegetation and soil with asphalt, concrete and roofing materials that absorb more solar energy than natural surfaces. The effect is strongest at night, when built surfaces release stored heat slowly, so neighborhoods with few trees can remain several degrees warmer than nearby rural land.

Planners have long assumed that street trees are the simplest remedy. A three-year study in the fictional city of Calder Falls tested this assumption by comparing two districts of similar size and population. In the first, the city planted 400 new trees along residential streets. The second district, which had a comparable density of buildings, received no new planting during the same period.

The results were less straightforward than the planners expected. Temperatures at street level fell by roughly two degrees Fahrenheit on shaded blocks during summer afternoons, but the reduction disappeared after dark. The researchers attribute this to the trees' limited canopy, which had not yet matured enough to trap heat rising from pavement. They also observed that the benefit depended heavily on irrigation, since young trees that lacked water provided little cooling at all.

The authors do not conclude that tree planting is ineffective. Instead, they argue that the timing of cooling benefits should be considered alongside the cost of watering, and that mature canopy, rather than the number of trees planted, may be the more useful measure of success. Their recommendations include combining planting with reflective pavement in the most exposed blocks.
